nameStory: The hairy-tailed mole gets its name from the distinctive feature that sets it apart from other moles - its tail is covered in coarse, visible hairs rather than being nearly naked like most moles. This furry tail is so characteristic that early naturalists made it the defining feature in the common name. It's also called Brewer's mole after Thomas Mayo Brewer, a 19th-century American naturalist who studied New England wildlife.
description: The hairy-tailed mole is a compact, underground mammal perfectly built for a life of tunneling through soil. About the size of a small hamster, it has velvety dark fur, enormous front paws shaped like shovels, and tiny eyes that are nearly invisible. Its most distinctive feature is its short tail covered in stiff, dark hairs - quite different from the nearly bald tails of other moles. This secretive creature spends almost its entire life in underground tunnels, rarely seen above ground except when dead on roads or found by cats.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, velvety fur that feels incredibly soft and appears dark gray to black, with each hair able to bend in any direction - an adaptation for moving forward or backward in tight tunnels

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact body about 5-7 inches long with a cylindrical shape, weighing roughly as much as two AA batteries, with a pointed snout and nearly invisible pinhead-sized eyes

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Enormous front paws with long, curved claws that create distinctive shovel-like prints much wider than the body, while hind feet are small and narrow

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Short tail (about 1 inch) densely covered with coarse, dark hairs that stick out visibly - unlike the nearly naked tails of other moles

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Creates raised ridges of soil (molehills) and surface tunnels that feel spongy underfoot, plus small volcano-shaped mounds of fine, dark earth pushed up from deeper tunnels

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Almost never seen alive above ground; when found on the surface they move with an awkward swimming motion, using their massive front paws to pull themselves along

habitat: Prefers well-drained soils in deciduous and mixed forests, woodland edges, and sometimes lawns and gardens with rich, loose earth. Avoids wet, clay-heavy soils and very sandy areas where tunnels would collapse. Most common in areas with plenty of earthworms and soil insects, from sea level to mountain slopes throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Most active near the surface as soil thaws and earthworms become abundant, creating fresh molehills and surface tunnels in lawns and gardens.
seasonality.summer: Tunneling activity moves deeper as surface soil dries out, though shallow tunnels remain visible as raised ridges in moist areas.
seasonality.fall: Increased surface activity as they prepare for winter, often creating new tunnel systems and prominent molehills in preparation for harsh weather.
seasonality.winter: Remains active under snow and frozen ground, working in deeper tunnel systems where soil doesn't freeze and some invertebrates remain available.

funFact: A single hairy-tailed mole can eat up to 100% of its body weight in earthworms and insects every single day - they literally cannot survive more than a few hours without food due to their incredibly fast metabolism.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with star-nosed moles, but hairy-tailed moles lack the bizarre fleshy star around the nose and have that distinctive furry tail. Eastern moles have nearly bald, scaly tails and are larger overall. Remember: hairy tail = hairy-tailed mole!
contextualKnowledge: Many people think moles eat plant roots and bulbs, but they're actually carnivores that only eat insects, worms, and other soil invertebrates. The plant damage blamed on moles is usually caused by voles (small rodents) that use abandoned mole tunnels as highways to reach roots.
compareHints: The hairy-tailed mole is the only species in its genus, making it unique among North American moles. Compared to other New England moles, it's intermediate in size - larger than the tiny star-nosed mole but smaller than the eastern mole. Its hairy tail immediately distinguishes it from both relatives, which have nearly naked tails.
